a: All the people gathered as one person
p: The chapter opens on the same words that close the list in 7:73 and begin Ezra 3. The date is the autumn feast month.
b: Nehemiah 7:73 ends the list of returning families with "the seventh month came, and the Israelites were in their towns," and Ezra 3:1 continues from the same words: "The seventh month arrived. The Israelites were in their towns, and the people gathered at Jerusalem, all together as one" (Ezra 3:1). On that shared seam, see the note on Ezra 2:70. Here the gathering leads not to an altar but to a book. The year is not given. If the chapter stands where the book puts it, this is October 445 BC, a few days after the wall was finished on the 25th of the sixth month (6:15). "As one person" (literally "as one man") describes a people of one mind, as in Judges 20:1.

a: They called on Ezra the scribe
p: Ezra appears suddenly, thirteen years after his arrival. Scholars debate whether Nehemiah 8 first stood in Ezra's story.
b: Ezra came in Artaxerxes' seventh year (Ezra 7:8). Here he reads the law in Nehemiah's day, and the story is told in the third person, like Ezra 10. Three views: (1) The canonical order is the real order, or at least a deliberate one: Ezra kept teaching after the marriage crisis, and the book sets his law-reading at the climax of the rebuilding (Kidner, Fensham, Eskenazi). (2) It once stood between Ezra 8 and Ezra 9: Ezra reads the law in his first autumn, and the officials then report the marriages (Torrey, Rudolph, Myers, Williamson; see the note on Ezra 9:1). (3) It once followed Ezra 10: 1 Esdras runs straight from the end of the divorce story into this reading (1 Esdras 9:37–55), and a minority of scholars take that as the older order, though 1 Esdras is selective and may simply have joined the two Ezra episodes. Those who date Ezra to 398 BC, after Nehemiah, must also explain Nehemiah's presence in 8:9 (see the note on 12:26). All three agree that the editor placed it here so that the law is read once the city is walled and its people are counted.

a: in the open square facing the Water Gate
p: The Water Gate stood on the east side of the city, toward the Gihon spring. The square was public ground, not Temple ground.
b: The Water Gate is placed on the east, near the Ophel (3:26), and probably took its name from the Gihon spring below. The square in front of it lay outside the Temple courts. That matters: women, and anyone else kept out of the inner courts, could hear the law here, and the reading is led by a scribe rather than offered as a rite at the altar. Many see in this scene the roots of the synagogue, where the community gathers around a scroll rather than a sacrifice. The same square is one of the places where booths are built (8:16).

a: the scroll of Moses' law
p: Sefer is a scroll, not a bound book. The book never says how much of the Torah it held.
b: The Hebrew sefer torat Mosheh is "the scroll of Moses' law"; codices with pages came centuries later, so "scroll" is used throughout these chapters. What the scroll contained is debated, and the main views are set out in the note on Ezra 7:14. Chapter 8 itself shows its readers finding the Booths law of Leviticus 23 (8:14) and the reading of Deuteronomy 31 (8:18), and 13:1 quotes Deuteronomy 23. That fits a scroll containing at least Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and most readers take it as the whole Torah. On torah, "law" in the sense of "teaching, instruction," see the note on Ezra 3:2.

a: men and women alike, and everyone able to listen with understanding
p: Deuteronomy told Israel to gather men, women and children to hear the law at the Feast of Booths. Ezra's crowd matches it.
b: Moses commanded a public reading every seventh year: "Call the people together, the men, the women and the children, and the foreigner who lives in your towns. Let them hear it and learn" (Deuteronomy 31:12). Ezra's reading falls in the same month and runs on through the feast (8:18). The phrase "everyone able to listen with understanding" probably means children old enough to follow, as the covenant list says again: "all who could know and understand" (10:28). The verb bin, "understand," runs through the chapter (8:2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 12): the point of the day is not only hearing but understanding. The rabbis took this as the model for the reading of the law in public (see 8:8).

a: It was the first day of the seventh month
p: The law makes the first of the seventh month a holy day of trumpet blasts. Jewish tradition keeps it as Rosh Hashanah.
b: Leviticus says: "In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you are to have a day of rest, a reminder made with loud blasts, a holy gathering" (Leviticus 23:24; compare Numbers 29:1). In later Jewish practice this day became Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, and the rabbis read 8:9–12 as a guide for keeping it: the day is holy, so not a day for mourning, even though it begins the Days of Awe that lead to the Day of Atonement. The text itself mentions no trumpets and no sacrifices. It records a holy day given over to hearing the law.

a: Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden tower
p: The Hebrew calls Ezra's platform a migdal, a "tower." It is the ancestor of the reading desk of the synagogue.
b: Migdal usually means a tower (12:38–39). Here it is a raised wooden stand, high enough for the whole crowd to see the scroll (8:5). 1 Esdras 9:42 calls it a wooden bema, "platform," the word later used for the raised reading desk of synagogues (the bimah) and of churches. Thirteen men stand with Ezra, six on the right and seven on the left. They are probably lay leaders, since the Levites are named separately in 8:7. The lists in 1 Esdras 9:43–44 differ in several names (they include Azariah and Hezekiah on the right), a reminder of how easily names changed in copying.

a: As he opened it, all the people rose to their feet
p: Jewish congregations still stand when the Torah scroll is raised and opened. The custom is traced to this verse.
b: The Talmud draws a rule from this verse: once the reader opens the scroll, people are not to speak, even about matters of law, for "opened" and "stood" go together (Bavli Sotah 39a). Standing became the people's sign of respect for the word read aloud. Churches that stand for the reading of the Gospel keep a similar custom, though it grew up separately. In the story, standing comes before any word is read: the people honor the scroll itself as God's word to them.

a: With their hands raised, all the people answered, "Amen, amen."
p: The doubled "Amen" seals a blessing or an oath. Raised hands and bowing complete the people's answer.
b: "Amen" comes from the root 'aman, "be firm, be true": to say it is to say "so it is" or "so be it." Doubled, it closes the first books of the Psalter (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:19; Psalm 89:52) and answers the oath in Numbers 5:22. Lifting the hands is a posture of prayer and praise (Psalm 134:2; Lamentations 2:19; 1 Timothy 2:8), and bowing with the face to the ground is the deepest form of reverence (2 Chronicles 7:3). The same root returns when the people make their "firm agreement" (amanah, 9:38).
r: Numbers 5:22; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 134:2; Lamentations 2:19; 1 Timothy 2:8; 2 Chronicles 7:3; 9:38

a: were giving the people understanding of the law
p: Teaching the law was an old Levite task. Here they move among the people and help them grasp it.
b: Moses' blessing gives Levi the work of teaching: "They will teach your rulings to Jacob and your law to Israel" (Deuteronomy 33:10). Chronicles remembers Levites sent out by Jehoshaphat who "taught in Judah, and they had with them the scroll of the LORD's law" (2 Chronicles 17:9), and Josiah's Levites "who taught all Israel" (2 Chronicles 35:3). Several of the thirteen named here lead the prayer in 9:4–5 and sign the covenant in 10:9–13. The Hebrew says "and the Levites," which could mean that the named men worked alongside other Levites, or that the named men were themselves the Levites; 1 Esdras 9:48 reads it the second way. The Greek of 2 Esdras names only three (see the variant).

a: explaining it as they went
p: The rare word mephorash has been read as "clearly," "section by section," or "with translation." Each changes the scene.
b: Mephorash means something "made distinct." Views: (1) Read clearly, distinctly, so all could hear (KJV "distinctly"). (2) Read in sections, with pauses for the Levites to explain each part. (3) Translated: the people now spoke Aramaic, and the Levites put the Hebrew into it. The Talmud takes this view: "explaining" is the Targum, the Aramaic translation; "they set out its meaning" is the division into verses; and "they grasped what was read" is the reading marks or the traditions of how to read (Bavli Megillah 3a; Bavli Nedarim 37b). (4) A Persian legal term for a document read and explained, as in Ezra 4:18 (see the note there). Many modern scholars combine (2) and (3). Christian preachers have long taken the verse as the model for preaching that reads a text and explains it.
orig: מְפֹרָשׁ וְשׂוֹם שֶׂכֶל (meforash ve-som sekhel), 'made distinct, and putting sense'

a: Then Nehemiah, who was the governor
p: The title is tirshata, a Persian word. The Greek versions lack it here, and 1 Esdras turns it into a man's name.
b: Tirshata is probably a Persian title meaning something like "the one to be respected." It is used of the governor of the first return (Ezra 2:63, where this site renders it "the governor") and of Nehemiah here and in 10:1. 12:26 uses the ordinary word for governor, pechah. The Greek of 2 Esdras has "Nehemiah" without the title, and 1 Esdras 9:49 has no Nehemiah at all: it reads the title as a name, "Attarates" (Codex Alexandrinus spells it Attharates). Many critical scholars, including Williamson and Blenkinsopp, think the words "Nehemiah, who was the governor" were added when Ezra's story was joined to Nehemiah's; others reply that the shorter readings are themselves secondary. See the variant on this verse.

a: For everyone had been crying as they listened to what the law said
p: The text does not say why the people wept. Readers have heard grief over sin, fear of the curses, or deep emotion.
b: Grief over sin: the law showed them how far they and their ancestors had fallen short, as when Josiah tore his clothes on hearing the scroll (2 Kings 22:11). The confession of chapter 9 supports this. Fear of the curses: Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 end with warnings of exile, and the hearers were living in what those chapters foretold. Overwhelming emotion: a scattered people hearing its own story read aloud in its own city. The leaders do not deny the grief; they postpone it. Confession has its day (9:1), but this day is a feast.

a: send shares to those who have nothing ready
p: Feasting includes the poor. The same custom, "sending portions," marks Purim in the book of Esther.
b: Deuteronomy's feasts are for the whole community, including the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow (Deuteronomy 16:14). Here the holy day is kept by eating well and by seeing that those with nothing prepared share in it. The phrase "sending portions" (mishloach manot) is the same custom that Esther 9:19 and Esther 9:22 set for Purim, when Jews send gifts of food to one another and to the poor. It is still kept on Purim today.

a: the joy of the LORD is your stronghold
p: Ma'oz is a place of refuge, a fortress. The usual English "strength" loses the picture of a safe place.
b: Ma'oz means a stronghold or refuge: "The LORD is the stronghold of my life" (Psalm 27:1, translated fresh; compare Psalm 28:8; Psalm 37:39). Nehemiah has just built walls for the city; now he tells the people that their real defense is "the joy of the LORD." That can mean the joy the LORD gives, the joy they take in the LORD, or the LORD's own joy over them (Zephaniah 3:17). Neither Greek version has "the joy of the LORD." 2 Esdras has "for he is your strength," and 1 Esdras 9:52 has "for the Lord will glorify you" (see the variant). Who speaks is also unclear. "He told them" may be Nehemiah, Ezra or the speaker of 8:9 as a group.
orig: כִּי־חֶדְוַת יְהוָה הִיא מָעֻזְּכֶם (ki chedvat YHWH hi ma'uzzekhem)

a: "Hush," they said
p: Has is a sound word, like English "shh." Elsewhere it calls for silence before God.
b: Has imitates the sound people make to quiet others. The prophets use it for awe before the LORD: "Hush before the Lord GOD" (Zephaniah 1:7, translated fresh; compare Habakkuk 2:20; Zechariah 2:13; Amos 6:10). Here the Levites use it to calm weeping, not to call for awe, and the reason is joy: "this day is holy." The Levites move through the crowd as pastors as well as teachers.

a: to gain insight into the words of the law
p: On the second day the leaders, not the crowd, gather to study. The scene looks ahead to later Jewish study of Scripture.
b: The verb lehaskil means "to gain insight, to understand deeply." The heads of families, the priests and the Levites come to Ezra as students to a teacher. What they find is a command that the whole people can carry out at once (8:14–15). This is what Ezra had set out to do: "For Ezra had given his heart to searching out the LORD's law, to doing it, and to teaching its rules and rulings in Israel" (Ezra 7:10). Jewish tradition traces to Ezra and the "Men of the Great Assembly" the study of the law that would become the work of the rabbis (Mishnah Avot 1:1).

a: the Israelites were to live in booths at the feast in the seventh month
p: What they find is Leviticus 23: Israel must live in booths for seven days to remember the wilderness.
b: The command is in Leviticus 23:42–43: "Live in booths for seven days. Everyone born in Israel is to live in booths, so that your descendants will know that I made the Israelites live in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 23:42–43). Deuteronomy names the Feast of Booths but does not command living in booths (Deuteronomy 16:13–15), and Ezra 3:4 says the first returnees kept the feast without mentioning booths. The people of Nehemiah's day find a part of the law they had not been keeping, and they act on it the same month. On the feast as a whole, see the topic page.

a: Bring back leafy boughs of olive, of oil tree, of myrtle, of palm and of thick-leaved trees
p: The proclamation is said to follow what is written, but no verse in the Torah gives these words or this list of trees.
b: Leviticus 23:40 says: "On the first day take for yourselves the fruit of beautiful trees, palm fronds, branches of thick-leaved trees and poplars of the valley stream" (Leviticus 23:40). Nehemiah's list shares palms and thick-leaved trees, adds olive, "oil tree" and myrtle, and leaves out the fruit and the poplars. Ets shemen, "oil tree," may be the wild olive or a resinous tree; the KJV has "pine," and the Greek of 2 Esdras has "cypress." Some read "as it is written" loosely, as a summary of Leviticus applied to new circumstances. The rabbis saw two separate laws: the four kinds of Leviticus 23:40 are held and waved in worship, while Nehemiah's branches were for roofing the booths, a distinction the Talmud discusses in tractate Sukkah. Others think Ezra's scroll had a form of the law we no longer have.
orig: עֲלֵי עֵץ שֶׁמֶן (alei ets shemen), 'leaves of oil tree'

a: each man on his roof
p: Flat roofs and courtyards were ordinary living space. The booths fill every open space in Jerusalem.
b: Houses had flat roofs reached by stairs, used for drying crops, sleeping in summer and prayer (Joshua 2:6; 1 Samuel 9:25; Acts 10:9). Booths go up on roofs, in courtyards, in the Temple courts and in two public squares: the Water Gate on the east (8:1) and the Gate of Ephraim on the north, which opened on the road toward Ephraim (2 Kings 14:13; 12:39). The list shows a city that was crowded for the feast, though it had few permanent residents (7:4; 11:1).

a: Not since the days of Jeshua son of Nun had the Israelites done it this way
p: The feast had been kept before, at Solomon's dedication and in Ezra 3. The claim is about how it was kept.
b: Solomon held the feast for seven days and seven more (1 Kings 8:65), and the first returnees "held the Feast of Booths just as it is written" (Ezra 3:4). So the claim is not that the feast was forgotten. It may mean that never since Joshua had the whole people lived in booths, or kept it with such joy, or done it so closely by the written law. The pattern "not since..." is used for great moments of reform, such as Josiah's Passover: "No Passover like this one had been held since the time of the judges" (2 Kings 23:22). "Jeshua" is the late Hebrew form of Joshua, found only here for Joshua son of Nun; it is the same name as Jesus (Greek Iesous).
r: 1 Kings 8:65–66; Ezra 3:4; 2 Kings 23:22; 2 Chronicles 30:26; 2 Chronicles 35:18; Joshua 1:1

a: He read aloud from the scroll of God's law every day
t: Reading at the feast, then and now
p: Deuteronomy commanded the law to be read at Booths. Jewish practice later ended the year's Torah reading at this season.
b: Deuteronomy 31:10–11 sets a public reading "when the Feast of Booths comes round," every seventh year. Here the reading runs every day of the feast. The eighth day, a "closing assembly" as Leviticus 23:36 and Numbers 29:35 call it, became Shemini Atzeret in Jewish practice; in time it was joined by Simchat Torah, "Rejoicing in the Torah," when the yearly cycle of synagogue readings ends with Deuteronomy and starts again with Genesis. The two feasts of law and joy in this chapter, the first of the month and the feast of booths, both end with the same thing: the scroll read and gladness.

a: This same month, on its twenty-fourth day
p: The feast ended on the 22nd. Two days later the mood turns from joy to fasting. The Day of Atonement is never mentioned.
b: The Feast of Booths ran from the 15th to the 21st, with the closing assembly on the 22nd (Leviticus 23:34–36). The fast on the 24th comes after the celebration the leaders had insisted on (8:9–11): the grief that was held back now has its day. Readers have long noticed that the Day of Atonement, on the 10th of this month (Leviticus 23:27), is passed over in silence. Some think it was kept and simply not reported, since the book follows the law-reading, not the Temple calendar. Others take the silence as a sign that chapters 8 and 9 were once separate stories joined by an editor. The fast itself is a voluntary act of the community, like those of Ezra 8:21 and Ezra 10:6.

a: dressed in sackcloth, with soil on them
p: Coarse goat-hair cloth and dirt on the head were the clothes of mourning and of prayer in disaster.
b: Sackcloth was rough cloth, often of goat hair, worn next to the skin as a sign of grief (Genesis 37:34; Jonah 3:5–8). Dirt or ashes on the head showed humiliation: after the defeat at Ai, Joshua and the elders "threw dust on their heads" (Joshua 7:6). The three signs together, fasting, sackcloth and dirt, mark the community's whole body as taking part in the confession that follows.
r: Genesis 37:34; Joshua 7:6; 1 Samuel 4:12; Jonah 3:5–8; Daniel 9:3; Matthew 11:21

a: Israel's offspring kept themselves apart from everyone of foreign birth
p: Before confessing, the people stand apart from foreigners. The point here is worship, not marriage.
b: "Israel's offspring" (zera Yisra'el) recalls Ezra 9:2, where "the holy seed" had mixed with the peoples of the lands. Here the separation comes before a confession of Israel's own sins and its ancestors' sins: this is a family confessing its history, and only members of the family speak. Nothing is said of divorce or expulsion. On the verb badal, "separate," and the door left open to outsiders who joined Israel (Ezra 6:21), see the note on Ezra 10:11. The pledge of 10:28 uses the same verb for those who "had kept apart from the peoples of the lands for God's law," which suggests that people of foreign birth could join.

a: for a fourth of the day
t: Three hours of reading, three of confession
p: A quarter of a day is about three hours. Reading and confession alternate, a pattern for later worship.
b: The day ran from dawn to dark, about twelve hours, so a quarter is about three hours. The people spend as long on the law as on confession, and the order matters: hearing the law comes first and leads into confessing. Ezra's own reading ran from first light until noon (8:3). The pattern of Scripture read, then answered in prayer, became the shape of synagogue worship and of the Christian service of the word.

a: Up on the Levites' stairway stood
p: The Levites stand on a raised place to lead. The names overlap with those who taught in 8:7.
b: Ma'aleh means "ascent, steps"; it was a raised place from which the Levites could be seen and heard, like Ezra's tower in 8:4. Two lists of eight names follow (9:4 and 9:5), with five names in both. Bani appears twice in 9:4, which may be a copying error or two men of one name. Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and Hodiah also taught in 8:7, and most of these names return among the Levites who sign the covenant (10:9–13). "A great cry" is a loud lament, as in the cries to God in Judges (Judges 3:9).

a: Get up! Bless the LORD your God from age to age!
p: The Levites' call turns into a prayer to God in the same breath. Its words echo the doxologies of the Psalms.
b: Doxologies close the books of the Psalter: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from age to age" (Psalm 41:13, translated fresh; compare Psalm 106:48 and 1 Chronicles 16:36). Here the Levites call the crowd to bless, and then, without a break, speak to God: "May people bless the name of your glory." The shift from "your God" (the people's) to "your glory" (God's) is where the prayer begins. The phrase "raised high above every blessing and praise" says that no human praise can reach God's worth. Jewish prayer echoes this line in the Kaddish, which praises God as "beyond every blessing and song."

a: It is you who are the LORD, and you alone
p: The Hebrew gives the prayer to the Levites. The Greek adds "And Ezra said." Others hear the voice of the whole people.
b: The Levites, named in 9:5, as the Hebrew reads: they lead, and the people answer. Ezra: the Greek of 2 Esdras opens 9:6 with "And Ezra said," and the RSV and NRSV follow it (see the variant). The people: the prayer says "we" throughout, and 9:38 has the people's leaders seal what "we" make. There is also the question of where it came from. Many scholars think it is an older liturgical prayer placed here by the editor. H. G. M. Williamson suggested that it was first used by Judeans who stayed in the land after 586 BC, since it says nothing of exile in Babylon or of the return. Mark Boda showed how closely it is woven from the Torah and the Prophets. Whatever its origin, it now stands where the community has just heard the law.

a: the heavens of the heavens and all their army
p: The prayer starts with creation. The stars that other nations worshiped are themselves worshipers of the LORD.
b: "The heavens of the heavens" is a Hebrew way of saying "the highest heavens": "Look: the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you" (1 Kings 8:27). "Their army" is the sun, moon and stars, which Israel was warned not to worship: "do not be pulled away to bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19). The prayer turns that around: "the army of the heavens bows low to you." The same phrase can also mean the angels (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 148:2). Only this prayer, among the confessions of the period, begins with creation: Israel's story is set inside the story of the world.
r: Deuteronomy 10:14; 1 Kings 8:27; Deuteronomy 4:19; 1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 148:1–6; Genesis 1:1; Genesis 2:1

a: who chose Abram, who brought him out from Ur of the Chaldeans and made his name Abraham
p: The story of Israel begins with God's choice of one man. Three phrases come straight from Genesis.
b: God "chose" (bachar) Abram, a verb Genesis does not use of him but Deuteronomy uses of Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6). "Brought him out from Ur of the Chaldeans" repeats God's words in Genesis: "I am the LORD, who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess" (Genesis 15:7). "Made his name Abraham" recalls Genesis 17:5: "No longer will you be called Abram. Abraham will be your name" (Genesis 17:5). Abraham's call to leave Mesopotamia is told again because the hearers' own families had just come back from there.
r: Genesis 11:31; Genesis 12:1; Genesis 15:7; Genesis 17:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; Joshua 24:2–3

a: You found his heart faithful toward you
p: Ne'eman, "faithful," comes from the same root as Genesis 15:6, "Abram put his trust in the LORD."
b: Genesis says: "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The prayer uses the same root, 'aman: God found Abram's heart ne'eman, faithful, steady, and so he "cut the covenant" of Genesis 15:18–21, naming the peoples of the land. The prayer lists six of them; Genesis 15 has ten. God in turn proved faithful: "You have made your words come true, for you are in the right." At the end of the prayer the people make their own amanah, "firm agreement" (9:38). Paul builds on Genesis 15:6 for faith in Romans 4 and Galatians 3; James 2:21–23 joins Abraham's faith to his obedience in Genesis 22.
r: Genesis 15:6; Genesis 15:18–21; Genesis 22:1–18; 9:38; Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23; Hebrews 11:8–10

a: because you knew they had been insolent toward them
p: The verb zid, "be insolent," describes Egypt here. The prayer then uses it twice for Israel.
b: Jethro used this verb of Egypt: "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods. He proved it when they acted with such pride against this people" (Exodus 18:11). The prayer applies it to Pharaoh's people here, and then twice to Israel's ancestors: "they, our ancestors, were insolent" (9:16) and "they were insolent and would not listen" (9:29). Mark Boda and others point out the effect: Israel came to behave toward God as Egypt had behaved toward Israel. "A name that is still yours today" means a reputation, as in Exodus 9:16, where God says he spared Pharaoh to make his name known in all the earth.

a: like a stone into mighty waters
p: The crossing is told in the words of Exodus 14 and of Moses' song in Exodus 15.
b: "The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground" (Exodus 14:22). Moses' song says of the Egyptians: "The deeps cover them. They went down to the bottom like a stone" (Exodus 15:5), and "Like lead they went under in the mighty waters" (Exodus 15:10). The prayer combines the two images. The Sea of Reeds in 9:9 is the same sea; on the name, see the topic.

a: Onto Mount Sinai you came down, and from the heavens you spoke with them
t: Down on the mountain, speaking from heaven
p: Exodus says both: God came down on Sinai, and spoke from the heavens. The prayer keeps both.
b: "The LORD came down upon Mount Sinai, onto the mountaintop" (Exodus 19:20), and afterward: "You have seen for yourselves that I spoke with you from the heavens" (Exodus 20:22). The prayer keeps both statements side by side. Deuteronomy explains it this way: God's voice came from heaven while his fire was on the earth (Deuteronomy 4:36). The four terms for what God gave, rulings, laws, rules and commands, are the Torah's own vocabulary; all four are called good, right or true. The Torah is presented as a gift, not a burden, before the prayer tells how Israel broke it.
r: Exodus 19:20; Exodus 20:22; Deuteronomy 4:36; Psalm 19:7–9; Psalm 119:137–138; Romans 7:12

a: You let them know your holy Sabbath
p: Of all the laws given at Sinai, only the Sabbath is named. That points ahead to 10:31 and 13:15–22.
b: In the prayer's summary of Sinai, the Sabbath alone is singled out, and it is "your holy Sabbath," God's own day. Israel had first kept it with the manna (Exodus 16:23–30), and it is the sign between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13–17; Ezekiel 20:12). By the Persian period, when Jews lived scattered among the nations without a king or an army, the Sabbath and circumcision had become the marks that set them apart. The covenant of 10:31 binds the people to it, and Nehemiah's last reforms fight for it (13:15–22).

a: the land that you had raised your hand to give them
p: Raising the hand was the gesture of an oath. God swore to give the land.
b: To raise the hand was to swear: "I will bring you to the land I lifted my hand in oath to give to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob" (Exodus 6:8; compare Numbers 14:30). Bread from the heavens and water from the rock recall Exodus 16:4 and Exodus 17:6. Jesus' hearers quoted this tradition, "He gave them bread from heaven to eat" (John 6:31, translated fresh, quoting Psalm 78:24), and Jesus answered that the true bread from heaven is himself (John 6:32–35). Paul calls the rock "Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).
r: Exodus 6:8; Numbers 14:30; Exodus 16:4; Exodus 17:6; Psalm 78:24; John 6:31–35; 1 Corinthians 10:3–4

a: in their rebellion they appointed a leader to go back to their slavery
p: The words recall Numbers 14:4, when the people wanted a new leader to take them back to Egypt.
b: At Kadesh, after the spies' report, the people said: "Let's appoint a leader and go back to Egypt" (Numbers 14:4). The prayer calls Egypt "their slavery": to wish to go back was to choose slavery over the God who freed them. In Numbers they only proposed it; the prayer says they did it, which sharpens the charge. The Hebrew "in their rebellion" differs by one letter from "in Egypt," the reading of the Greek and of some Hebrew manuscripts (see the variant). The God who answers this rebellion is the God of Exodus 34:6 (see the next note).

a: But you are a God of forgiveness, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love
p: The prayer quotes the words God spoke to Moses after the golden calf, the most quoted creed in the Hebrew Bible.
b: After the golden calf, the LORD passed before Moses and proclaimed: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The words return in Numbers 14:18, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8 and Psalm 145:8, and twice in this prayer (9:17, 9:31). The prayer adds "a God of forgiveness," literally "a God of forgivenesses" (eloah selichot), a rare plural also in Daniel 9:9. Jewish penitential prayers are called Selichot, and they are built around the thirteen attributes of Exodus 34:6–7, so this verse stands close to the heart of Jewish prayer for forgiveness.
orig: אֱלוֹהַּ סְלִיחוֹת (eloah selichot), 'a God of forgivenesses'
r: Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 86:15; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Daniel 9:9; 9:31

a: 'This is your god, who brought you up from Egypt.'
p: Exodus has "These are your gods." The prayer has the singular: "This is your god."
b: Exodus reports: "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (Exodus 32:4), and Jeroboam says the same of his two calves (1 Kings 12:28). The Hebrew elohim can mean "God" or "gods," and in Exodus the verb is plural. The prayer has zeh eloheikha, "this is your god," with a singular verb. Some see this as a way of making clear that one calf was meant, or that the people meant it as an image of the LORD, since Aaron called out, "Tomorrow is a festival for the LORD!" (Exodus 32:5). Others think the prayer simply retells freely. Either way the prayer calls it "great acts of contempt" (ne'atsot), a word used for despising God (Numbers 14:11).
orig: זֶה אֱלֹהֶיךָ (zeh eloheikha), 'this is your god'
r: Exodus 32:1–6; Exodus 32:4; Exodus 32:5; 1 Kings 12:28; Numbers 14:11; Psalm 106:19–20; Acts 7:41

a: To give them insight you gave your good Spirit
p: The Spirit given in the wilderness may recall the elders who prophesied with Moses. Christians hear the Holy Spirit.
b: In Numbers God says of the seventy elders: "I will draw off some of the spirit that is on you and put it on them" (Numbers 11:17), and they prophesied. Isaiah 63:10–14 also speaks of God's holy Spirit among the people in the wilderness, and Psalm 143:10 prays, "Let your good Spirit lead me" (translated fresh). The prayer links the Spirit with "insight" (haskil), the same verb used of the leaders' study in 8:13. Jewish readers usually take this as the spirit of prophecy given to Moses and the elders. Christian readers have seen here the Holy Spirit, who teaches (John 14:26).

a: Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell
p: The words repeat Deuteronomy 8:4. Moses said them to teach Israel that people live by every word from God.
b: Moses said: "Your clothes did not wear out on you, and your feet did not swell, these forty years" (Deuteronomy 8:4; compare Deuteronomy 29:5). In Deuteronomy the point is that the wilderness taught Israel to depend on God's word, not on bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3), the verse Jesus quoted when he was tested in the wilderness (Matthew 4:4). The prayer's summary, "they were short of nothing," echoes Deuteronomy 2:7.

a: you shared those out to them, corner by corner
p: The Hebrew is short and unclear. It may mean God gave Israel every corner of the land, or set the peoples as borders.
b: Literally, "you divided them to a corner." Readings: (1) God shared out the conquered kingdoms to Israel, "corner by corner," that is, completely. (2) God allotted the peoples to Israel "as a boundary" (pe'ah can mean an edge or border). (3) God scattered the nations "into corners," driving them away, a meaning some find in Numbers 24:17. The Plain English Translation takes (1). The Hebrew has "the land of Sihon and the land of the king of Heshbon." Since Sihon was king of Heshbon (Numbers 21:26), the Plain English Translation reads the "and" as "that is," and many think the second "land of" is a copying slip; 2 Esdras has only "the land of Sihon king of Heshbon" (checked). The first conquests named are those east of the Jordan, over Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan (Numbers 21:21–35), which the Psalms celebrate (Psalm 135:10–12; Psalm 136:17–22).
r: Numbers 21:21–35; Deuteronomy 2:24–3:11; Psalm 135:10–12; Psalm 136:17–22; Numbers 24:17; Numbers 21:26

a: You made their sons many, like the stars of the heavens
p: God had told Abraham to count the stars. The prayer says the promise came true in Egypt and the wilderness.
b: "Look toward the sky and number the stars, if you can number them... So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5). Moses told Israel that the promise had come true: God had made them "as many as the stars of the sky" (Deuteronomy 1:10; Deuteronomy 10:22). The prayer joins the promise of offspring (9:23) to the promise of land (9:24–25), the two halves of what God swore to Abraham in 9:8. The sons are the generation that entered the land, not the one that died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:31).

a: They ate and were full and grew fat, and they lived in luxury on your great goodness
p: The verse borrows Deuteronomy's picture of the good land, and its warning that a full stomach forgets God.
b: Moses promised "houses full of all kinds of good things that you did not fill, wells cut in the rock that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant," and warned, "When you eat and are full, watch yourself. Do not forget the LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:11–12). The Song of Moses foretold the result: "Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked" (Deuteronomy 32:15). The verb "lived in luxury" (vayyit'addenu) comes from the root of Eden, "delight": Israel enjoyed a garden-like land. The next verse turns at once to rebellion, as Deuteronomy said it would.

a: Your prophets, who testified against them to turn them back to you, they killed
p: The charge that Israel killed its prophets runs from Kings to the New Testament. Stephen makes it in Acts 7.
b: Elijah complains: "They have killed your prophets with the sword" (1 Kings 19:10). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned "in the courtyard of the LORD's house" (2 Chronicles 24:21), and Uriah was killed by Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20–23). Jesus takes up the charge: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killer of the prophets" (Matthew 23:37), and Stephen's speech in Acts 7, which retells Israel's history much as this prayer does, ends with it (Acts 7:52). "They threw your law behind their backs" uses the image of 1 Kings 14:9, where God says to Jeroboam, "me you threw behind your back" (1 Kings 14:9).
r: 1 Kings 18:4; 1 Kings 19:10; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Jeremiah 26:20–23; Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:51–52; 1 Kings 14:9; Ezekiel 23:35

a: you gave them rescuers, and they rescued them from their foes' power
p: These verses tell the book of Judges in brief: sin, oppression, a cry, a rescuer, rest, then sin again.
b: Judges repeats a cycle. Israel sins; God hands them to enemies; they cry out; God raises "a rescuer for them, and he rescued them" (Judges 3:9); and when the judge dies, "they would go back and behave worse than their ancestors" (Judges 2:19). The prayer keeps the Hebrew wordplay of "foes" (tsarim) who "pressed them hard" (yatseru) in their "time of pressure" (tsarah). It also adds what Judges leaves implied: God "listened from the heavens," the phrase of Solomon's prayer for Israel in trouble (1 Kings 8:30–39). "Time and again" (9:28) answers anyone who thinks God's patience runs out after one rescue.

a: the ones that, if a human being does them, he will live by them
p: The prayer quotes Leviticus 18:5. Ezekiel repeats the line, and Paul quotes it twice.
b: Leviticus says: "Keep my rules and my rulings. If a human being does them, he will live by them" (Leviticus 18:5). Ezekiel uses the line three times in his review of Israel's history in the wilderness (Ezekiel 20:11; Ezekiel 20:13; Ezekiel 20:21), and the prayer follows the same pattern: the law was given for life, and Israel turned from it. The rabbis read it as "live by them, and not die by them," so that saving a life overrides most commands (Bavli Yoma 85b). Paul quotes it to contrast the law's way with righteousness by faith (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12); others read Paul as contrasting two ways of using the same law. Christians differ on how Paul's use relates to its sense in Leviticus.
r: Leviticus 18:5; Ezekiel 20:11; Ezekiel 20:13; Ezekiel 20:21; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12; Luke 10:28

a: They gave you a defiant shoulder
t: A shoulder that will not take the yoke
p: The picture is of an ox that shrugs off the yoke. Zechariah uses the same phrase.
b: Katef soraret is "a stubborn (defiant) shoulder," the shoulder of a work animal that refuses the yoke: "Israel has been stubborn, as stubborn as a heifer" (Hosea 4:16, translated fresh). Zechariah uses the identical phrase of the generation before the exile: "they gave a defiant shoulder" (Zechariah 7:11, translated fresh). A "stiff neck" is the same picture from another angle (9:16–17), and the phrase is Moses' own description of Israel (Exodus 32:9; Deuteronomy 9:6). Jesus' invitation uses the other side of the image: "Lift my yoke onto yourselves" (Matthew 11:29).
r: Hosea 4:16; Zechariah 7:11; Exodus 32:9; Deuteronomy 9:6; 2 Kings 17:14; Matthew 11:29–30

a: You testified against them by your Spirit, by the hand of your prophets
t: The Spirit spoke through the prophets
p: The prayer explains the prophets as the voice of God's Spirit, as Zechariah 7:12 also does.
b: Kings sums up the warning: "Yet the LORD had given warning to Israel and to Judah by every prophet and every visionary" (2 Kings 17:13). Zechariah adds that the words were sent "by his Spirit through the earlier prophets" (Zechariah 7:12). The prayer joins the two: God's Spirit (9:20) taught in the wilderness and then spoke through the prophets. Christians later confessed the Holy Spirit as the one "who spoke through the prophets" (the Nicene Creed, AD 381; compare 2 Peter 1:21). "The peoples of the lands" here are the Assyrians and Babylonians.

a: you did not wipe them out, and you did not desert them
p: Even the exile was not the end. The prophets had promised that God would not make a full end of his people.
b: Jeremiah's warnings carry the same limit: "I will not make a full end" (Jeremiah 4:27; Jeremiah 5:10; Jeremiah 5:18, translated fresh). The prayer's hearers are the proof that God kept it: a remnant lived through the exile and returned. The verse repeats "gracious and compassionate" from 9:17, so that God's character frames the whole history of rebellion. On the remnant, see the topic and Ezra 9:8.

a: the great, mighty and fearsome God, who keeps the covenant and loyal love
p: The titles come from Deuteronomy 10:17 and Deuteronomy 7:9. Nehemiah's first prayer and Daniel's prayer use them too.
b: Moses called the LORD "the great, mighty and fearsome God" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and said: "He keeps his covenant and his loyal love for a thousand generations with those who love him" (Deuteronomy 7:9). Nehemiah's own prayer opens with the same words (1:5), and so does Daniel's (Daniel 9:4). The Talmud says the "Men of the Great Assembly" earned their name here: Jeremiah had stopped calling God "fearsome" and Daniel had stopped calling him "mighty," and this prayer restored the full title (Bavli Yoma 69b). After more than twenty verses of history, this is the prayer's only request: "let none of the hardship... seem small in your sight." It does not ask outright for freedom or for the empire's fall. It asks God to look.

a: since the days of the kings of Assyria until this day
p: From the Assyrian kings of the 700s BC to the Persians, Israel had lived under foreign empires for about 300 years.
b: Assyria's kings first made Israel pay tribute in the 700s BC (2 Kings 15:19–20), destroyed Samaria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6) and besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC (2 Kings 18–19). Babylon followed, then Persia. The prayer counts all of it as one long hardship, still going on "until this day." On the use of "Assyria" for the Persian empire in Ezra 6:22, see the note there.

a: Yet you are in the right in all that has come on us
p: In the middle of its pain, the prayer says God has been fair. This is the heart of the biblical confession.
b: The prayer gives no complaint against God: "You have done what is faithful, and we have done what is wicked." Ezra's prayer ends the same way, "LORD, God of Israel, you are in the right" (Ezra 9:15), and so does Daniel's (Daniel 9:7; Daniel 9:14). Gerhard von Rad called this pattern a "doxology of judgment": the guilty give glory to God by admitting that his judgment was just (compare Joshua 7:19). Many readers find here a model of honest repentance that does not blame God. Others, reading beside Job and the lament psalms, note that the Bible also lets sufferers protest. The two are not opposed in the prayer itself, which confesses guilt and still asks God to see the hardship (9:32).
r: Ezra 9:15; Daniel 9:7; Daniel 9:14; Joshua 7:19; Lamentations 1:18; Psalm 51:4; Job 9:2

a: Here we are today: slaves!
p: The prayer calls Persian rule slavery. Readers differ on whether that is protest, confession, or both.
b: Ezra's prayer thanks God for the Persian kings' kindness while still calling the people slaves (see the note on Ezra 9:9). This prayer is sharper: the harvest of their own land goes to foreign kings. Some hear political protest, a voice from those who paid the taxes of chapter 5. Others stress that the prayer blames Israel's sins, not Persia, for the situation (9:37: "for our sins"). Others, with Williamson, note that the prayer never mentions the return from exile or the rebuilt Temple, and suggest it was first prayed by Judeans who lived under foreign rule in the land itself. Deuteronomy had warned: "A people you have never known will eat what your soil grows" (Deuteronomy 28:33).

a: Our bodies are theirs to rule, and our cattle too, as they like
p: Persian kings taxed produce and could call up men and animals for labor or war.
b: Persian subjects paid tribute and "the king's tax" (5:4; Ezra 4:13), and the empire could requisition workers, soldiers and pack animals. Herodotus describes the levies of men from every province for Xerxes' war against Greece (Herodotus 7.61–99). "Over our bodies" probably means such forced service. The community's own governor was himself the king's officer.

a: we are making a firm agreement and writing it down
p: The people do not use berit, "covenant," but amanah, from the root of "Amen" and of Abraham's faithful heart.
b: Amanah appears only here and in 11:23 in this sense. It comes from 'aman, "be firm," the root of "Amen" (8:6) and of Abraham's "faithful" heart (9:8). God had kept his word; now the people bind themselves in writing to keep theirs. Why not berit, the usual word for covenant? Some say the people could not make God's covenant, only pledge to keep it. Others think amanah was a legal term of the period for a binding written agreement. In content it is a covenant renewal, like those under Joshua, Jehoiada, Hezekiah and Josiah (Joshua 24:25; 2 Kings 11:17; 2 Chronicles 29:10; 2 Kings 23:3). On the sealed copy, see the chapter 10 page.

a: On the sealed copies were
p: Important documents were rolled, tied and sealed with clay stamped by each witness's seal.
b: Jeremiah describes the custom: a purchase deed was written, witnessed and sealed, with an open copy kept beside it (Jeremiah 32:10–14). Hundreds of small clay seal impressions (bullae) survive from Judah, and the Wadi Daliyeh papyri from Samaria, written in the 300s BC, were found still tied and sealed. Here the leaders' names are "on the sealed copies" (plural in Hebrew), perhaps one seal for each signer. The governor signs first, as the representative of the king's authority; the Greek of 2 Esdras gives no title here, as in 8:9.

a: and Zedekiah
p: Zedekiah signs second, before the priests. He was probably Nehemiah's secretary, though the text does not say.
b: Zedekiah stands alone between the governor and the priests. Many commentators think he was Nehemiah's scribe or secretary, a chief official who signed for the governor's office, and some connect him with "Zadok the scribe" of 13:13, since Zadok can be a short form of the same name. Others think he was simply a leading layman. The book gives nothing more.

a: Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah
p: The 21 priestly names of 10:2–8 are mostly family names. They match the lists of 12:1–7 and 12:12–21 closely.
b: Most of these names reappear as the heads of priestly houses in 12:1–7 (the first return) and 12:12–21 (Joiakim's day): Seraiah, Jeremiah, Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, Shebaniah (Shecaniah in 12:3), Harim (Rehum in 12:3), Meremoth (Meraioth in 12:15), Obadiah, Ginnethon, Abijah, Mijamin (Miniamin in 12:17), Maaziah (Maadiah and Moadiah in 12:5, 12:17), Bilgai (Bilgah), and Shemaiah. So the signers are probably heads of houses signing for their families. Daniel and Hattush came with Ezra (Ezra 8:2). Two great houses are missing: Jedaiah and Joiarib, the first two divisions in 1 Chronicles 24:7 and listed in 1 Chronicles 9:10, and the four large families of Ezra 2:36–39 appear only as Pashhur and Harim. No explanation is given.

a: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel
p: Jeshua, Binnui and Kadmiel head the Levites in every list of the period. Many of the rest taught in 8:7.
b: The first return counted the Levites as "descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel" (Ezra 2:40), and Henadad's line helped rebuild the Temple and the wall (Ezra 3:9; 3:18). Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan and Sherebiah were among those who explained the law (8:7) or led the prayer (9:4–5). The signers, then, are the same men who taught the people what they were now promising to keep.

a: The heads of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani
t: Clans, men and even a town
p: The lay list starts with the clans of Ezra 2 in the same order, then moves to individual names, many from the wall list in chapter 3.
b: The first names follow the list of returning families nearly in order: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani, then Azgad, Bebai, Adonijah (Adonikam in Ezra 2:13), Bigvai, Adin, Ater and Hezekiah. In Ezra 2:16 "Ater, of Hezekiah" is one family; here the two names stand apart. Anathoth (10:19) is a town (Ezra 2:23). After about twenty clan names come individuals, several of them builders of the wall: Meshezabel and Meshullam (3:4), Hasshub (3:11, 3:23), Hallohesh (3:12), Rehum (3:17). The list shows the community signing both as families and as persons.

a: everyone who had kept apart from the peoples of the lands for God's law
t: Joining for the sake of the law
p: The signers include those who had separated themselves to God's law. Many read this as including converts.
b: The same phrase in Ezra 6:21 describes those "who had separated himself to them from the uncleanness of the nations of the land, to seek the LORD" (Ezra 6:21), and joined the returned exiles at Passover. Here it may mean Israelites who had kept clear of foreign ways, or people of non-Israelite birth who joined Israel by taking on its law. Many commentators see the second sense in both verses, and so a door that stays open for those who choose the LORD (see the note on Ezra 10:11). Others take it as the returnees and those Judeans who had never been exiled but now joined them. Wives, sons and daughters are counted, as at the reading of the law (8:2).

a: They take on themselves a curse and an oath
p: To enter a covenant under a curse meant calling down disaster on yourself if you broke it.
b: Alah, "curse," and shevu'ah, "oath," go together: one swears and accepts the curse that will fall on the breaker. Deuteronomy pairs "the covenant of the LORD your God and his curse-oath" (Deuteronomy 29:12), and Daniel's prayer says the exile came because "the curse and the oath written in Moses' law" had been poured out (Daniel 9:11, translated fresh). The people now step back under the same terms. "Their brothers, their leading men" are the nobles who signed (10:14–27): the rest of the people "stand firmly with" them, adding their own oath to the leaders' seals.

a: our daughters we will not give to the peoples of the land
p: The pledge applies Deuteronomy 7:3, which named the nations of Canaan, to "the peoples of the land" of the writers' own day.
b: Deuteronomy says: "Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons" (Deuteronomy 7:3). There the ban covers the seven nations of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:1), and the reason is religious: "they will turn your sons away from following me" (Deuteronomy 7:4). The pledge puts "the peoples of the land" in their place, as Ezra 9:1–2 and Ezra 9:12 had done. This is the first of the covenant's terms, and the first broken again (13:23–27). On how the Bible treats such marriages and how Ezra and Nehemiah differ, see the topic on foreigners and the note on 13:25.

a: we will take nothing from them on a Sabbath or a holy day
p: The Torah forbids work on the Sabbath but never mentions buying. The covenant spells out what keeping it means.
b: The Sabbath law says: "Do no work on it: not you, not your son or your daughter... not the foreigner who lives in your towns" (Exodus 20:10). It does not mention trade. Amos had condemned traders who could not wait for the Sabbath to end (Amos 8:5), and Jeremiah forbade carrying loads through the gates (Jeremiah 17:21–22). The covenant draws the line at buying from non-Jews who are not bound by the law. David Clines showed that many terms in this chapter work this way: they take a written law and decide how to apply it to a new case, an early example of the reasoning later called halakhah. Traditional readers see faithful application; some critics see the beginnings of legalism; many Jewish readers see the necessary work of keeping an old law alive.

a: We will let the seventh year go, and let go of every loan
p: One verb joins two laws: letting the land lie fallow (Exodus 23) and cancelling debts (Deuteronomy 15).
b: Exodus says of the land: "in the seventh year let it go and leave it alone, so that the needy of your people can eat from it" (Exodus 23:11). Deuteronomy says of loans: "Every lender is to let go of the loan he made to his neighbor" (Deuteronomy 15:2). The covenant uses the Exodus verb (natash) for both and so reads the two laws as one sabbatical year. After the debt crisis of chapter 5, where families had pledged fields and children (5:1–13), the pledge to cancel debts was not abstract. The sabbatical year was kept in later times: 1 Maccabees 6:49–53 tells of a food shortage in Jerusalem because it was a seventh year.

a: a third of a shekel a year
p: Exodus asks half a shekel at a census. The covenant sets a yearly third of a shekel. Later Judaism paid a half shekel each year.
b: Exodus 30:13 says: "Everyone who crosses over to join those enrolled will give this: half a shekel, by the holy place's shekel" (Exodus 30:13). That was a payment at a census. The covenant makes a yearly tax of a third. Explanations: the shekel in use was heavier than the old one; the people were poor (5:1–5); or the Exodus rule was being applied freely to a new need, since the Persian grants for the Temple were no longer enough (Ezra 6:9; Ezra 7:20–22). By the time of Jesus every Jewish man paid a half shekel a year, the tax Peter was asked about (Matthew 17:24–27). The Mishnah devotes a tractate, Shekalim, to it.

a: for the bread set in rows
p: "The bread of the row" is the twelve loaves set out before the LORD every Sabbath.
b: Leviticus 24 describes it: "Set them in two rows, six to a row, on the table of pure gold before the LORD" and "Sabbath after Sabbath he is to set it in order before the LORD, always" (Leviticus 24:6; Leviticus 24:8). The KJV calls it "the showbread." The list that follows runs through the Temple's year: the daily offerings, Sabbaths, new moons, feasts and the sin offerings that make atonement. The covenant pays for the whole calendar. Jesus recalled David eating this bread when he was hungry (1 Samuel 21:6; Mark 2:25–26).

a: As for the wood offering, we, the priests, the Levites and the people, have cast lots
t: A wood offering the Torah does not name
p: The law says the altar fire must never go out, but not who supplies the wood. The covenant decides by lot.
b: Leviticus says: "Fire is to keep burning on the altar without a break. It is not to go out" (Leviticus 6:13). Someone had to bring the wood. The covenant turns that need into a duty "as it is written," an example of what Clines calls exegesis: drawing out what a law implies. The custom lasted. The Mishnah lists nine days in the year when named families brought the wood (Mishnah Taanit 4:5), and Josephus mentions a festival of wood-carrying in his own day (Jewish War 2.425). The Temple Scroll from Qumran also describes a wood festival.

a: we will bring the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle
p: Firstborn sons were not offered on the altar. They were bought back with a payment to the priests.
b: The law claims every firstborn for God (Exodus 13:2) but adds: "Among your sons, you will ransom every human firstborn" (Exodus 13:13). Numbers sets the price: "It is five shekels of silver by the shekel of the holy place" (Numbers 18:16). So "bringing" a firstborn son meant bringing the redemption money, as Mary and Joseph did when they presented Jesus (Luke 2:22–24). Jewish families still keep the ceremony of pidyon haben, "redemption of the son." Clean animals were offered; unclean ones such as donkeys were bought back too.

a: The tithe of our ground we will bring to the Levites
p: The law gave the tithe to the Levites, who gave a tenth of it to the priests. The covenant puts that into practice.
b: Numbers says: "To the descendants of Levi, look, I give every tithe in Israel as an inheritance" (Numbers 18:21), and the Levites were to "set aside from it a gift for the LORD, a tenth of the tithe" (Numbers 18:26). The covenant adds the practical point: the Levites collect it in the farming towns, with a priest present (10:38), and carry the priests' tenth to the Temple storerooms. Malachi, probably from the same period, accuses the people of robbing God and says: "Bring the entire tithe into the storehouse" (Malachi 3:10). Chapter 13 shows the system breaking down (13:10–12).

a: We will not desert our God's house
p: The covenant ends with the pledge that sums it up. Chapter 13 asks whether it was kept, using the same verb.
b: The verb is azav, "leave, desert." The prayer uses this verb four times: three times God did not desert his people (9:17, 9:19, 9:31), and once he left them to their enemies for a time (9:28); the people now promise not to desert his house. When Nehemiah comes back, he asks the officials: "Why is God's house deserted?" (13:11), with the same verb. Haggai had made the same complaint a century earlier: the people lived in good houses while God's house lay in ruins (Haggai 1:4; Haggai 1:9).

a: they drew lots so that one in ten would come to live in Jerusalem
t: A tenth of the people for the city
p: Jerusalem had walls but few houses. The people cast lots to move one family in ten into it.
b: "The city was spread out wide and was big, yet only a few people lived inside it, and the houses were not built yet" (7:4). A walled city with no one in it could not be defended. Moving people into a capital was a known practice in the ancient world; Greek cities called it synoikismos, "settling together." The lot left the choice to God: "People throw the lot into the lap, / but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Setting aside one in ten is like a tithe of the people for the holy city. The story begun in 7:4–5 picks up here after the reading of the law and the covenant.

a: the holy city
p: Nehemiah is the first narrative book to call Jerusalem "the holy city." The name lasted into the New Testament.
b: Isaiah had used the name in prophecy (Isaiah 48:2; Isaiah 52:1), and here it enters ordinary narrative (11:1, 11:18). Daniel's seventy weeks are decreed for "your people and your holy city" (Daniel 9:24). Matthew calls Jerusalem "the holy city" (Matthew 4:5; Matthew 27:53), and Revelation sees "the holy city, new Jerusalem" coming down from God (Revelation 21:2). Today the Arabic name of Jerusalem, al-Quds, also means "the holy."

a: every man who freely volunteered to settle in Jerusalem
p: Were the volunteers the ones chosen by lot, or others who went without being chosen?
b: Some read the volunteers as an extra group, people who offered themselves on top of those chosen by lot, and the people blessed them for it. Others think 11:2 describes how those chosen by lot accepted willingly. The verb hitnaddev is used for freewill offerings (Ezra 1:6; Ezra 2:68) and for volunteers in war (Judges 5:2): to move to the city was a kind of offering. Living in Jerusalem was not easy: it meant leaving family land and living in a city surrounded by enemies (4:7–8).

a: Here are the provincial leaders who lived in Jerusalem
p: The list of Jerusalem's residents in 11:3–19 closely parallels 1 Chronicles 9:2–17, with different numbers and some different names.
b: Both lists move from Judah and Benjamin to the priests, Levites and gatekeepers, and many names match. The numbers differ: Benjamin's men are 928 here (11:8) and 956 in 1 Chronicles 9:9; the priests total 1,192 here (11:12–14) and 1,760 in 1 Chronicles 9:13. Chronicles adds people from Ephraim and Manasseh (1 Chronicles 9:3) and Zerahites (1 Chronicles 9:6); Nehemiah lists Perez and Shelah. Some think both lists adapt one older register (Williamson); others think Chronicles drew on Nehemiah; Sara Japhet argued that each writer reshaped the list for his own purposes. The servants of Solomon are explained in the note on Ezra 2:55.

a: of the descendants of Perez
p: Judah's clans came from his sons Perez, Zerah and Shelah. David's line ran through Perez.
b: Judah's sons were Shelah, Perez and Zerah (Genesis 38; 1 Chronicles 2:3–4). Perez was the ancestor of Boaz and David (Ruth 4:18–22). Nehemiah's list names descendants of Perez (11:4–6), of Shelah (11:5, see the note there) and of Zerah (11:24); 1 Chronicles 9:4–6 has the same three. Perez is also in the line of Jesus (Matthew 1:3).

a: son of the Shilonite
p: The Hebrew vowels say "the Shilonite," a man from Shiloh. Many read "the Shelanite," a descendant of Judah's son Shelah.
b: Shiloh was in Ephraim, an odd home for a man of Judah. The same consonants read with different vowels give "the Shelanite," from Shelah, Judah's third son, whose clan Numbers 26:20 calls "the Shelanites." With that reading the verse completes the three clans of Judah (see the note on 11:4). 1 Chronicles 9:5 has the same problem ("the Shilonites"). Many translations, among them the BSB ("a descendant of Shelah"), take the Shelah reading. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew vowels, which the Greek of 2 Esdras also follows ("son of the Seloni").

a: and after him Gabbai and Sallai: 928
p: "After him Gabbai, Sallai" is odd. Many scholars think it once read "and his brothers, men of valor."
b: The list has given Sallu's family tree (11:7) and then adds "and after him Gabbai, Sallai" with a number. In the parallel lines for the priests the pattern is "and their brothers... capable men" (11:12, 11:14). With small changes to the letters, gabbai sallai could be gibborei chayil, "men of valor," and "after him" could be "his brothers." Several commentators adopt that, and the Greek of 2 Esdras has two names (Gebi, Seli), which shows the Hebrew had these letters early. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

a: Judah son of Hassenuah was next in charge of the city
t: Second in charge, or over the Second District?
p: Mishneh can mean "second" in rank or the "Second District" of Jerusalem, a newer quarter of the city.
b: Huldah the prophet "lived in Jerusalem in the second district" (2 Kings 22:14), and Zephaniah mentions a wail from "the Second" (Zephaniah 1:10). So the Hebrew al ha'ir mishneh may mean that Judah was over the Second District, as the BSB has it, or that he was second-in-command of the city under Joel. The Greek of 2 Esdras reads "second over the city." The father's name has the article in Hebrew, hassenu'ah, as in 1 Chronicles 9:7.

a: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin
p: 1 Chronicles 9:10 lists Jedaiah, Jehoiarib and Jachin as three priests, not father and son.
b: The parallel has "Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin" (1 Chronicles 9:10). Joiarib and Jedaiah were the first two of the twenty-four priestly divisions, and Jachin the twenty-first (1 Chronicles 24:7; 1 Chronicles 24:17). "Son of" here may have come in by a copying slip, or may mean that Jedaiah's house descended from Joiarib's. The Hasmonean kings, Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, came from the house of Joiarib (1 Maccabees 2:1).

a: the officer in charge of God's house
p: Seraiah's title, nagid of God's house, names the chief officer of the Temple. It is the same title as in 1 Chronicles 9:11.
b: Seraiah's family tree runs through Zadok and Ahitub, the high priestly line (compare Ezra 7:1–2). 1 Chronicles 9:11 has "Azariah son of Hilkiah" with the same ancestors and the same title, "the officer in charge of the house of God" (1 Chronicles 9:11). Seraiah and Azariah were both names in the line, so the two lists may name different generations. Nagid is used of a king designate in Samuel; here, as in Jeremiah 20:1, it is a Temple official.

a: Their officer was Zabdiel son of Haggedolim
p: Haggedolim means "the great ones." It may be a name, or a way of saying Zabdiel came from a leading family.
b: Haggedolim has the article: "the great ones." As a personal name it would be unusual. Some read "son of one of the great men," that is, of a leading family; others keep it as a name, as most English versions do. The Greek of 2 Esdras has only "Badiel" with no father. The same verse calls the 128 priests gibborei chayil, "strong and capable men," an army phrase used here for men able in their work.

a: Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the heads of the Levites
p: The Greek of 2 Esdras has much shorter lists in chapters 11 and 12. It leaves out whole verses and many names.
b: As checked in 2 Esdras 21–22 (Rahlfs' text): in chapter 11 the Greek has no 11:16, 11:20, 11:21, 11:28, 11:29 or 11:32–35. It has only short forms of 11:30 (Lachish and its fields ... in Beersheba) and 11:31 (from Geba, Michmash). In 11:14 it has "Badiel" with no father's name. In 11:17 it drops Mattaniah's title and Bakbukiah. In chapter 12 it keeps only Shecaniah in 12:3, has no 12:4–6, lacks the four names of 12:7, and has no names in 12:9. In 12:41 it has Benjamin for Miniamin, and in 12:42 it has "and they were mustered" in place of "with Jezrahiah in charge" (see the variants). Most scholars think the translator or his Hebrew copy shortened the lists, since the Hebrew names fit the parallel lists (10:2–8; 12:12–21; 1 Chronicles 9). Some think a few of the Hebrew lists grew after the Greek was made. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew throughout.

a: the leader who began the thanks at prayer
p: The Hebrew is compressed. Mattaniah led the thanksgiving that opened the prayers. Some change one letter to read "head of the praise."
b: Literally, "head of the beginning, he gave thanks at the prayer." Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph, seems to have started or led the singing of thanks in worship. A small change (hattehillah for hattechillah) gives "head of the praise," which some prefer. The verse names two of the three singer families that Chronicles traces to David: Asaph (through Mattaniah) and Jeduthun (through Abda). Heman's line is not named. Bakbukiah is "second." On Jeduthun's name, see the variant. The Greek of 2 Esdras drops "the leader who began the thanks at prayer; Bakbukiah, the second among his brothers" and goes straight to Abda (see the note on 11:16).

a: The Ophel was where the temple servants lived
p: The Ophel was the swelling ridge between the City of David and the Temple Mount.
b: Ophel means "swelling, bulge." It names the high ground just south of the Temple, between it and the older City of David, and it had been walled since the days of the kings (2 Chronicles 27:3; 2 Chronicles 33:14). Living there put the temple servants next to their work. On who the temple servants (netinim) were, see the note on Ezra 2:43.

a: For the king's command was over them
p: The king who gave orders for the singers may be David, or the Persian king who had freed Temple staff from taxes.
b: David: the book says twice that the singers served "as David the man of God had commanded" (12:24; compare 12:45 and 1 Chronicles 25:1). The Persian king: Artaxerxes' letter forbade any tax on "the singers, the gatekeepers, the temple servants" (Ezra 7:24), and the next verse speaks of the man who stood "at the king's hand" (11:24), clearly the Persian king. "A firm agreement" (amanah) is the word used for the covenant in 9:38; here it is a fixed arrangement for the singers' daily support.

a: stood at the king's hand in every matter that concerned the people
p: Pethahiah represented the people's affairs to the Persian king, or served as the king's official for Judah.
b: "At the king's hand" means at his service. Many think Pethahiah was Judah's representative at the Persian court, handling the community's business there, much as Nehemiah had served in Susa (1:11). Others think he was a royal officer in Jerusalem, responsible to the king for local matters. Either way, the verse shows that the community's life ran through the empire's officials. He was of the clan of Zerah, Judah's son (Genesis 38:30).

a: in Kiriath-arba and its villages
t: A real map, or an old one?
p: The southern towns reach to Hebron and Beersheba, outside the Persian province of Judah. Readers explain this in different ways.
b: Kiriath-arba is the old name of Hebron: "Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba" (Joshua 14:15). The list in 11:25–30 reads like Joshua 15, from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom. Yet the evidence from archaeology, gathered by Charles Carter and Oded Lipschits, and the wall list of chapter 3 suggest that the province of Yehud ended near Beth-zur, north of Hebron, and that the south was then Idumean, that is, Edomite, land. Some conclude that Judeans lived in scattered villages beyond the border. Others read the list as a claim to the old land of Judah, drawn from older lists rather than the borders of the day. Others date the list to a later time. "Its villages" is literally "its daughters," the small places around a town.

a: So they camped from Beersheba as far as the Valley of Hinnom
p: The verb is the wilderness word for pitching camp. It gives the settlement a temporary, pilgrim feel.
b: Vayyachanu, "they camped," is the verb of Israel's journey in Exodus and Numbers (Exodus 13:20; Numbers 33). Here it describes people settled in towns, perhaps because they lived as a small group among others, or perhaps to suggest that the return was a second entry into the land. Beersheba was the old southern limit ("from Dan to Beersheba," Judges 20:1), and the Valley of Hinnom was the border of Judah and Benjamin just south of Jerusalem (Joshua 15:8).

a: the Valley of Craftsmen
p: The Valley of Craftsmen is the place 1 Chronicles 4:14 names Ge-harashim, near Lod and Ono.
b: Chronicles explains the name: "Seraiah fathered Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, for they were craftsmen" (1 Chronicles 4:14). Lod (Lydda) and Ono lay on the edge of the coastal plain. Ono was where Sanballat and Geshem tried to lure Nehemiah (6:2). Lydda appears in Acts, where Peter heals Aeneas (Acts 9:32–35).

a: These are the priests and the Levites who came up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and with Jeshua
p: The list goes back to 538 BC. Its Ezra and Jeremiah are priestly houses, not the scribe or the prophet.
b: The list names 22 heads of priests from the days of Jeshua, the first high priest after the exile (Ezra 3:2). The "Ezra" in 12:1 and 12:13 and the "Jeremiah" are family heads of that generation: Ezra the scribe came about eighty years later, and Jeremiah the prophet was taken to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:6). The same houses appear, with small changes of spelling, in Joiakim's day (12:12–21) and among the signers of 10:2–8 (see the note on 10:2). Ezra 2:36–39 counts only four priestly clans for the first return, which suggests that these 22 were subdivisions or that the lists come from different times. The Greek of 2 Esdras has no text for 12:4–6, keeps only one name in 12:3 and none in 12:7 (see the note on 11:16).

a: Iddo, Ginnethoi, Abijah
p: Iddo's house produced the prophet Zechariah. Abijah's division was the one Zechariah the father of John the Baptist served in.
b: Zechariah the prophet was "son of Berechiah, son of Iddo" (Zechariah 1:1), and Ezra 5:1 calls him "son of Iddo" (see the note there). In Joiakim's day the head of Iddo's house was a Zechariah (12:16), and many identify him with the prophet. Abijah's house was the eighth priestly division (1 Chronicles 24:10); Luke says Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, belonged to it (Luke 1:5). Ginnethoi is the Hebrew form here; 10:6 and 12:16 have Ginnethon.

a: who led the songs of thanks, he and his brothers
t: Songs of thanks, sung in turn
p: Huyyedot, a rare word, means songs of thanksgiving. The Levites sang them in two groups facing each other.
b: Huyyedot, from the verb hodah, "give thanks," occurs only here. Mattaniah led them (see 11:17), and the next verse has Bakbukiah and Unni "facing them, watch by watch." 12:24 describes the same arrangement: "watch answering watch." This is antiphonal singing, one group answering another, a style seen in psalms with refrains (Psalm 136) and in the two choirs of 12:31–40. The custom of choirs singing in alternation was later taken up in synagogues and in churches.

a: Jeshua fathered Joiakim, Joiakim fathered Eliashib
p: Six generations of high priests reach from 538 BC to Jaddua, whom Josephus places in the time of Alexander the Great.
b: Jeshua served at the return (Ezra 3:2), Joiakim after him (12:26), and Eliashib in Nehemiah's day (3:1; 13:28). An Aramaic letter from Elephantine in Egypt, written in 407 BC, mentions "Johanan the high priest" in Jerusalem (see Ezra 10:6). Josephus says Jaddua was high priest when Alexander the Great came to Jerusalem in 332 BC (Jewish Antiquities 11.302–347). If he is right, this list was finished long after Nehemiah. Some conclude that the book was completed in the Greek period. Others think Josephus mixed up two men of the same name or shortened the line, and that the list ends in the late 400s. Frank Moore Cross proposed that names were repeated in the family (papponymy), so that two Johanans and two Jadduas may be missing.

a: Joiada fathered Jonathan
p: 12:22–23 name Johanan in this place in the line. Jonathan here may be a slip for Johanan.
b: The list of 12:22 runs "Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua," and 12:23 calls Johanan "son of Eliashib." Here Joiada's son is Jonathan (Yonatan). The two names differ by one or two letters in Hebrew, and most scholars think both mean the same man, the Johanan of the Elephantine letter. "Son of Eliashib" in 12:23 would then mean grandson, as "son" often does in genealogies. The Greek of 2 Esdras also has Jonathan here.

a: for Miniamin; for Moadiah, Piltai
p: The Hebrew gives no head for the house of Miniamin. A name dropped out early in copying.
b: Every other line in 12:12–21 has a house and its head. For Miniamin the head is missing. The Greek of 2 Esdras also has no name there, and it reads Moadiah as words, "at the appointed times," which shows that the gap is old. The Plain English Translation does not fill it. Miniamin is the Mijamin of 12:5 and 10:7.

a: up to the reign of Darius the Persian
p: This may be Darius II (423–404 BC) or Darius III (336–330 BC). The title "the Persian" may point to a writer after Persian rule.
b: Darius II: the list ends with Johanan, high priest in 407 BC by the Elephantine letter, and Jaddua, who could have served by about 400 BC. Darius III: if Josephus is right that Jaddua met Alexander (see the note on 12:10), the list reaches the last Persian king. Calling him "Darius the Persian" suggests to many that the writer lived after the Persians had fallen, when a Darius needed to be identified. Traditional readers date it to Darius II and see the list as updated by a later scribe after Nehemiah's memoir was written.

a: in the scroll of the annals
p: The "scroll of the annals" is a Temple record of the Levite families, not the biblical book of Chronicles.
b: Sefer divrei hayyamim, "the scroll of the matters of the days," is the same phrase as the Hebrew title of Chronicles. Here it names an official record, like the royal annals cited in Kings. It shows that the writer used registers kept by the Temple. On Johanan "son of Eliashib" and his room in the Temple, see the notes on 12:11 and Ezra 10:6.

a: as David the man of God had commanded
p: Only Chronicles and Nehemiah call David "the man of God." They credit him with ordering the Temple's music.
b: "Man of God" is usually a title for prophets such as Moses, Samuel and Elijah. Chronicles and Nehemiah give it to David as the one who ordered the Temple's worship: "for that was the command of David the man of God" (2 Chronicles 8:14), and compare 12:36. Chronicles describes David dividing the Levites and singers (1 Chronicles 23–26). Some think "Jeshua son of Kadmiel" was once "Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel," since these three lead the Levites in 10:9 and 12:8, and the Greek of 2 Esdras has "Jeshua and the sons of Kadmiel."

a: the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe
p: Only three verses set Ezra and Nehemiah side by side (8:9; 12:26; 12:36). They are central to the debate over Ezra's date.
b: If Ezra came in 458 BC and Nehemiah in 445 BC, the two men could have worked together, as these verses say. Scholars who date Ezra to 398 BC, after Nehemiah, think the names were joined by the editor: in 8:9 the Greek versions lack Nehemiah's title or name, in 12:36 Ezra's name can be read as an addition; and in 12:47 2 Esdras lacks "and in the days of Nehemiah" (see the variant there). Those who keep the traditional order reply that the book's own claim should stand unless it is shown false, and that Nehemiah's memoir, which is about walls and reforms, had no reason to mention a priest's teaching work. The arguments are set out on the Ezra 7 page.

a: Joiakim son of Jeshua
p: Judith's high priest is Joakim, the Greek form of Joiakim, the high priest who served after the return.
b: The book of Judith, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, sets its story soon after the exiles came home and made the temple holy again (Judith 4:3). Its high priest is "Joakim, the high priest who was then in Jerusalem" (Judith 4:6). He leads the defense of the hill towns and later comes to honor Judith (Judith 15:8). Joakim is the Greek spelling of Joiakim, the son of Jeshua named here and in 12:10. So the name fits the years after the return. Yet the same book calls Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians in Nineveh. Most scholars read Judith as a story that borrows real names, not as a record of events.

a: When the wall of Jerusalem was to be dedicated
p: The wall was finished in 445 BC (6:15). The dedication may have followed at once or years later.
b: Chanukkah, "dedication," is the word for opening a building for its purpose (Deuteronomy 20:5; 1 Kings 8:63; Ezra 6:16), and it gave its name to the later feast of Hanukkah, which celebrated the rededication of the Temple in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:56–59; John 10:22). Nehemiah's memoir resumes here in the first person (12:31). Many think the dedication followed soon after the wall was finished, and that chapters 8–11 have been placed between them. Others think it came later in Nehemiah's first term, after the city was settled (11:1–2), which is the order the book now has.

a: with cymbals, lyres and harps
p: The same three instruments appear whenever Chronicles describes the Levites' music.
b: David told the Levites to play "musical instruments, lyres, harps and cymbals" (1 Chronicles 15:16), and Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun "prophesied with lyres, harps and cymbals" (1 Chronicles 25:1). The nevel and kinnor were both stringed instruments, and scholars are not sure which was larger; this site renders nevel "lyre" and kinnor "harp," as in Chronicles. Cymbals kept the beat; priests blew the trumpets (12:35, 12:41). See the topic on music.

a: The singers' guild came together
p: "Sons of the singers" means members of the singers' families or guild, not only their children.
b: In Hebrew "son of" often means "member of a group": "sons of the prophets" were prophets in training (2 Kings 2:3). The singers lived in villages near Jerusalem, at Netophah near Bethlehem, Beth-gilgal, Geba and Azmaveth, where they could farm and still come to the Temple for their turns of service. Ezra 2:41 counts 128 singers, all descendants of Asaph; 7:44 has 148.

a: Then they made the people clean, and the gates and the wall
p: Purifying people was familiar. Purifying gates and a wall is unique, and the text does not say how it was done.
b: Priests and Levites purified themselves before holy work by washing, keeping apart from what defiled, and sometimes by sacrifice (2 Chronicles 29:15–19; Ezra 6:20). The people too were purified, as before Sinai (Exodus 19:10). But no law tells how to purify a wall. Some think it was sprinkled, as with the water for cleansing in Numbers 19. Others see a new idea: the whole city, not only the Temple, is now treated as holy ground, "the holy city" (11:1). The same idea appears when Levites guard the city gates on the Sabbath (13:22).
