a: set two great thanksgiving choirs in place, with their processions
p: Two choirs walk the top of the new wall in opposite directions and meet at the Temple.
b: The text does not say where the choirs began. Most think it was in the west, near the Valley Gate (2:13; 3:13), from which one went south and east by the Dung Gate and the Spring Gate (12:31, 12:37), and the other north past the Gate of Ephraim and the Sheep Gate (12:38–39). Both ended in the Temple (12:40). The route traces the gates of chapter 3 in reverse. A psalm invites the same walk: "Circle Zion, walk all around her. Count up her towers" (Psalm 48:12). Where Joshua's Israel marched around Jericho's walls until they fell (Joshua 6), these people march on their own walls to praise God for raising them.

a: Ezra the scribe walked at their head
p: This is the only place in Nehemiah's first-person memoir where Ezra appears.
b: The line has been read in two ways. As history: Ezra led one choir and Nehemiah followed the other (12:38), the priest and the governor sharing the day. As an editor's addition: the clause is short, it comes at the end of the verse, and the matching description of the second choir names no leader but Nehemiah, so many critical scholars think it was added to join the two leaders. See the note on 12:26. The instruments "of David the man of God" recall Hezekiah's reform, where Levites stood "with David's instruments" (2 Chronicles 29:26).

a: set off the other way
p: The Hebrew lemo'l, "opposite, in front," is often emended to "to the left," to match "to the right" in 12:31.
b: As written, lemo'l means "in front of, opposite": the second choir went in the opposite direction. Emended to lismo'l, "to the left," by adding one letter, the verse balances 12:31, where the first choir goes "to the right"; the BSB and many modern versions read it this way. The Greek of 2 Esdras has "meeting them," which reads the Hebrew as "toward" the first choir. The Plain English Translation's "the other way" fits both the written text and the emendation.

a: by the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Sheep Gate
p: The north wall's towers appear in the prophets. The Sheep Gate is where John's Gospel places the pool of Bethesda.
b: Jeremiah promised that the city would be rebuilt "from the Tower of Hananel" (Jeremiah 31:38), and Zechariah names it in his vision of Jerusalem secure (Zechariah 14:10). Both towers guarded the north side, the only side without a deep valley (3:1). The Sheep Gate, near the Temple, was rebuilt by the high priest (3:1). John places the pool of Bethesda "by the Sheep Gate" (John 5:2). The Gate of the Guard is otherwise unknown; it may be the Inspection Gate of 3:31.

a: Jerusalem's gladness could be heard from far off
p: "Joy" appears five times in one verse. It answers Ezra 3, where joy and weeping could not be told apart.
b: The Hebrew uses the root samach, "be glad," five times. At the founding of the Temple, "No one could tell the glad shouting apart from the weeping of the people, because the people shouted so loudly that the noise carried far away" (Ezra 3:13). Now the sound carries again, and this time it is only joy. Women and children are named as rejoicing, as they were named as hearers of the law (8:2). This is the high point of the book. The next verses begin to set up the problems of chapter 13.

a: For Judah's joy was in the priests and the Levites who stood in service
p: The covenant's promises (10:35–39) now get officials. The happy mood of the day carries into the giving.
b: Men are appointed over the storerooms for the gifts the covenant promised: first fruits, tithes and contributions (10:35–39). "The shares the law gives" are the portions the Torah sets for priests and Levites (Numbers 18). The narrator explains the generosity by the day's joy. The same storerooms are the setting of chapter 13: one has been turned into a room for Tobiah (13:4–5), and the Levites' shares have stopped (13:10). The sequence is deliberate: a description of how things should work comes just before the account of how they failed.

a: In the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah
p: The summary joins the first return to Nehemiah's day and leaves Ezra out.
b: The verse pairs Zerubbabel, the governor of the first return, with Nehemiah, the governor of the wall, as times when the community supported its Temple staff well. Ezra is not named. The main Greek witness, 2 Esdras, lacks "and in the days of Nehemiah" (see the variant), so in the Greek the verse looks back to Zerubbabel alone. That may be a scribe's slip from one "in the days of" to the next, or an older, shorter form to which Nehemiah's name was later added. Some read this as a sign that the summary came from a source that knew nothing of Ezra, or put him later. Others note that the verse is about governors who paid for the Temple, which Ezra, a priest, was not. Either way it presents an ideal, and the next chapter shows it slipping.

a: no Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of God, ever
p: Nehemiah quotes Deuteronomy 23:3–5 with small changes: "God" for "the LORD," and "ever" without the ten generations.
b: Deuteronomy says: "No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of their descendants may ever enter the assembly of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 23:3). Nehemiah's text has "the assembly of God" and keeps only "ever." Ezra had used the next verse of the same law to support his reform (Deuteronomy 23:6; see the note on Ezra 9:12). What "enter the assembly" meant was debated. It may mean full membership in Israel, a place in worship, or marriage into Israel. The rabbis read it as a ban on marriage with Ammonite and Moabite men only, which kept room for Ruth (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3). Isaiah 56:3–7 promises foreigners who keep the Sabbath a place in God's house, a text often set beside this one.

a: and he hired Balaam against them to curse them
p: The verse uses Deuteronomy 23:4–5. Balaam, hired to curse, could only bless.
b: Deuteronomy gives the reasons: "For they did not come to meet you with bread and water on the road when you came out of Egypt. And Moab hired Balaam son of Beor" (Deuteronomy 23:4), and "The LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you" (Deuteronomy 23:5). As in the Hebrew of Deuteronomy, the verb "he hired" is singular: Moab, or its king Balak. The story is in Numbers 22–24, where God tells Balaam, "Do not curse the people, because they are blessed" (Numbers 22:12). Balaam became a byword in the New Testament for leading God's people astray for profit (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14).
r: Deuteronomy 23:4–5; Numbers 22:1–24:25; Numbers 22:12; Joshua 24:9–10; 2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14

a: they set apart from Israel all the mixed crowd
p: 'Erev is the word for the "mixed crowd" that left Egypt with Israel. Here it names people of foreign descent in the community.
b: Exodus says: "A large mixed crowd also went up with them" (Exodus 12:38). The word recurs for foreign groups living among a people (Jeremiah 25:20; Jeremiah 50:37). Here it names those of mixed or foreign descent. The law read was about Ammonites and Moabites, but the action is wider. What "set apart" meant in practice is not said: exclusion from the assembly for worship, as Deuteronomy says; loss of full membership in the community; or expulsion. The text does not report anyone being sent away, except Joiada's son (13:28). On how these verses have been judged, see the chapter page.

a: Earlier, Eliashib the priest had been given charge of the storeroom of our God's house
p: The high priest of Nehemiah's day was Eliashib (3:1). This Eliashib may be the same man, or a priest in charge of the stores.
b: The high priest: Eliashib rebuilt the Sheep Gate (3:1), and his grandson married Sanballat's daughter (13:28), so his family's ties to Nehemiah's opponents fit. A different priest: the high priest would not usually be the storekeeper, and the verse calls him only "the priest." "Close to Tobiah" can mean related by marriage; Tobiah had ties to leading families through marriage (6:17–18). On Tobiah, an Ammonite official (2:10), see the notes on chapters 2 and 6. Placing an Ammonite in a Temple room right after the reading of 13:1 is the narrator's irony.

a: In the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, king of Babylon
p: Nehemiah went back to the king in 433/432 BC, after twelve years as governor. How long he stayed away is not said.
b: Nehemiah came in Artaxerxes' twentieth year (2:1) and governed twelve years, to the thirty-second (5:14), that is, 445 to 433/432 BC. Then he returned to court. "At the end of a stretch of days" he came back; most estimates put his return within a few years, before Artaxerxes died in 424 BC. Persian kings were also called "king of Babylon," as Cyrus is in Ezra 5:13: "in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon" (Ezra 5:13). The Greek of 2 Esdras keeps the title.

a: I threw all of Tobiah's household goods outside, out of the room
p: Nehemiah throws out the furniture of the man who had moved into God's house. Christians have compared Jesus clearing the Temple.
b: The act is personal and physical, like Nehemiah's later blows (13:25). Christian readers have often set it beside Jesus driving the traders from the Temple courts and overturning their tables (John 2:13–17; Mark 11:15–17). Both scenes defend the Temple from those using it for their own ends, and both show anger that some readers admire and others question. Nehemiah then has the rooms purified and the holy things put back (13:9), restoring them to the use the covenant had promised (10:37–39).

a: had run off to his own field
p: When the tithes stopped, Levites and singers went back to their farms to live. The Temple's service suffered.
b: The Levites had no tribal land of their own (Numbers 18:23–24), but some had fields around their towns (Numbers 35:2–5; 12:29). Without tithes, they had to farm. Malachi, probably writing in the same period, says the people were robbing God in tithes and contributions, and the storehouse was empty (Malachi 3:8–10). The covenant had promised exactly what failed here (10:37–39).

a: "Why is God's house deserted?"
p: Nehemiah's question uses the verb of the covenant's last line: "We will not desert our God's house."
b: The people had sworn "We will not desert our God's house" (10:39). Nehemiah's question uses the same verb, azav. Chapter 13 tests the covenant's promises one by one: the Temple storerooms (10:37–39; 13:4–14), the Sabbath (10:31; 13:15–22), and marriages (10:30; 13:23–27). Each had been broken. "I had it out with" renders rib, "contend, bring a complaint," the verb of a lawsuit (13:17; 13:25; 5:7).

a: These men were counted trustworthy
p: The new treasurers are a priest, a scribe, a Levite and a layman. Their qualification is that they can be trusted.
b: The four come from each group with a stake in the stores: Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, Pedaiah the Levite, and Hanan, probably a layman or a singer (his grandfather Mattaniah may be the singer of 11:17). Ne'emanim, "trustworthy," is from the root of the "firm agreement" (9:38) and of Abraham's "faithful" heart (9:8). Hezekiah had made the same kind of appointment over the Temple stores (2 Chronicles 31:11–15), and Paul says that what is required of stewards is that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2).

a: My God, remember me for this
p: Nehemiah's memoir is punctuated by short prayers that God remember him. They also resemble inscriptions of Persian-period officials.
b: The prayer recurs at 5:19, 13:14, 13:22 and 13:31; prayers that God remember Nehemiah's enemies come at 6:14 and 13:29. In the Bible, God's "remembering" means acting, as when God remembered Noah (Genesis 8:1). Joseph Blenkinsopp compared the inscription of Udjahorresnet, an Egyptian official who served the Persian kings and asked the gods to remember the good he had done for a temple. Nehemiah writes for God as much as for readers. "The loyal love I have shown" is chasadai, his acts of hesed: the same word as God's "great loyal love" in 13:22. The rabbis' criticism of this refrain is discussed on the chapter page and at 13:31.

a: In those days I saw men in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath
p: Nehemiah's Sabbath reform follows Jeremiah's sermon at the gates, almost point by point.
b: Jeremiah stood at the city's gates and said: Do not carry a load on the Sabbath day or bring it in through the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 17:21, in summary). If they obeyed, kings would enter by those gates; if not, God would "kindle a fire in its gates" (Jeremiah 17:27). Nehemiah sees loads coming in through the gates (13:15), reminds the nobles that their ancestors' Sabbath-breaking brought the disaster (13:18), and shuts the gates (13:19). Treading grapes was heavy work; it was the harvest season, when stopping for the Sabbath cost most. The covenant had banned buying (10:31). Here the people of Judah are working and selling as well.

a: The Tyrians living there were bringing fish
p: Phoenician merchants from Tyre had a trading colony in Jerusalem. Fish came from the coast, salted or dried.
b: Tyre was the great Phoenician trading city on the coast, and its merchants worked across the Persian empire (Ezekiel 27). Tyre and Sidon had supplied cedar for the second Temple (Ezra 3:7). The Fish Gate (3:3; 12:39) may have been named for this trade. Tyrians were not bound by the Sabbath, so the question was whether Judeans would buy from them on that day, the case the covenant had foreseen (10:31). "And in Jerusalem at that" stresses that this happened in the holy city itself.

a: When the gates of Jerusalem grew dim before the Sabbath
p: The Sabbath ran from evening to evening, so the gates were shut as night fell on Friday.
b: Leviticus sets the Day of Atonement "from evening to evening" (Leviticus 23:32), and Jewish practice has always reckoned the Sabbath the same way, from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday. Nehemiah closes the gates as the shadows fall and keeps them shut until it ends. The practice of beginning the Sabbath with the lighting of lamps before dark, still kept in Jewish homes, stands in the same tradition of guarding the day's edges. Jesus' burial was hurried for the same reason (Luke 23:54).

a: and to come and stand guard at the gates, to keep the Sabbath day set apart as holy
p: Levites guarded the Temple gates. Now they guard the city gates too, as if Jerusalem were a sanctuary.
b: Levites who were gatekeepers kept the Temple gates (11:19; 1 Chronicles 9:17–27). Nehemiah gives them the city gates for the Sabbath, after they purify themselves as for Temple duty. The phrase "to keep the Sabbath day set apart as holy" echoes the commandment: "Remember the day of the Sabbath, and set it apart as holy" (Exodus 20:8). With 12:30, where the gates and the wall are purified, this suggests that the whole city now shares the Temple's holiness. Nehemiah closes with a prayer for pity "as your great loyal love allows": he asks to be judged by God's hesed, not by his own record.

a: I saw Jews who had taken Ashdodite, Ammonite and Moabite women into their homes
p: Ezra's covenant sent foreign wives away. Nehemiah forbids new marriages but, as told, ends none of the existing ones.
b: The verb is the same one Ezra used: "We have taken foreign wives into our homes" (Ezra 10:2). Ashdod was the Philistine coastal province west of Judah; its people are named with Nehemiah's enemies in 4:7. The two reforms differ. Ezra leads a covenant to send away the wives and the children (Ezra 10:3; Ezra 10:11), with a court to judge cases. Nehemiah rebukes, curses and beats some of the men and makes them swear not to arrange such marriages for their children or themselves (13:25); he drives out only the priest married to Sanballat's daughter (13:28). On the whole subject, and on readings of both, see the topic on foreigners.

a: They could not speak Judean
p: "Judean" is the Hebrew of Judah. Children who spoke only Ashdodite or other tongues could not understand the law read aloud.
b: In 701 BC the officials of Hezekiah asked the Assyrian envoy, "Don't talk with us in Judean while the people on the wall are listening" (2 Kings 18:26). "Judean" (Yehudit) is Hebrew as spoken in Judah. "Ashdodite" was probably a local dialect, perhaps Aramaic or a late form of the Philistine coast's speech. For Nehemiah the danger was not only identity: a child who could not speak Hebrew could not join in the reading of the law (8:2–3, 8:8) or in the prayers. Later Judaism met the same problem by translating Scripture into Aramaic and Greek (see 8:8).

a: I cursed them, hit some of the men and tore at their hair
p: Readers have judged Nehemiah's methods very differently: as courage for a fragile community, or as cruelty.
b: On Ezra's opposite reaction, pulling out his own hair, see the note on Ezra 9:3. Nehemiah acts as governor, with physical punishment that the law allowed judges to give (Deuteronomy 25:2–3), and he takes an oath from the men. Defenders, among them Derek Kidner and H. G. M. Williamson, see a small community, a province of perhaps twenty or thirty thousand people with a capital of a few thousand at most, surrounded by stronger neighbors, whose language and faith were at real risk (13:24), and note that he stops short of breaking up families. Critics, such as David Janzen and Harold Washington, see the power of a governor used to draw ethnic lines, with women and children paying for men's decisions, and set the scene beside Ruth and Isaiah 56. Jewish tradition honors the reform but criticizes Nehemiah's self-regard (see 13:31).

a: Isn't this the very thing Solomon king of Israel sinned over?
p: Nehemiah cites 1 Kings 11: even the greatest king, loved by God, was led astray by foreign wives.
b: Kings tells it: "King Solomon gave his love to many women from foreign nations," among them women of Moab and Ammon, and "By the time Solomon was old, his wives had bent his heart to follow other gods" (1 Kings 11:1; 1 Kings 11:4). Nehemiah adds praise drawn from elsewhere: no king was his equal (1 Kings 3:12–13), and he was dear to God: "The LORD loved the boy" (2 Samuel 12:24), who was named Jedidiah, "loved by the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:25). The argument runs from the greater to the lesser: if Solomon fell, who is safe? Readers have noted that Solomon's son and heir Rehoboam had an Ammonite mother (1 Kings 14:21).

a: had become son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite
p: A grandson of the high priest married the daughter of the governor of Samaria. Josephus tells a similar story set a century later.
b: Sanballat was governor of Samaria; an Elephantine letter of 407 BC mentions "Delaiah and Shelemiah, the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria" (see the A lens). A priest of the high priestly family married to his daughter tied the Temple to Nehemiah's chief opponent, and Leviticus 21:14 required the high priest to marry "a virgin from his own kin." Josephus tells a similar story set a century later (see the next note). Yitzhak Magen, who excavated Mount Gerizim, dates a first sanctuary there to the mid-400s BC from coins and pottery, which would make the Samaritan temple older than Josephus says; some scholars place that first phase later.

a: Sanballat the Horonite
p: Two later sources name a Sanballat in Samaria. They should not be merged with Nehemiah's opponent without argument.
b: The Samaria papyri from Wadi Daliyeh, legal documents of about 375–335 BC hidden by refugees from Alexander's army, include a seal impression that reads "[...]iah son of [San]ballat, governor of Samaria," and a papyrus that names Hananiah as governor. Frank Moore Cross concluded that the name ran in the family and proposed a Sanballat II in the early 300s; others think the seal's Sanballat may be Nehemiah's opponent, named as the family's founder. Josephus tells of Manasseh, brother of the high priest Jaddua, who married Nikaso, daughter of a Sanballat sent to Samaria by Darius III, and for whom a temple was built on Mount Gerizim with Alexander's leave (Jewish Antiquities 11.302–347). Cross called him Sanballat III; no document outside Josephus names him. Some think Josephus retold the incident of 13:28 a century too late; others think a similar marriage happened twice in a family that kept the name.

a: the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites
p: Nehemiah appeals to God's covenant with the priests, the same idea that Malachi uses in his charge against them.
b: God gave Phinehas "a covenant of priesthood for all time, because he was zealous for his God" (Numbers 25:13), after Phinehas killed an Israelite man and a Midianite woman (Numbers 25:6–8). Malachi speaks of God's "covenant with Levi" and accuses the priests of corrupting it (Malachi 2:4–8, translated fresh in the sense), in what may be the same period. Nehemiah's prayer that God "remember against them" leaves judgment to God, as in 6:14.

a: My God, remember me for good
t: The last words: humility or self-praise?
p: The book, and in the Leningrad Codex the whole Hebrew Bible, ends with Nehemiah's prayer to be remembered.
b: The Talmud's criticism: Sanhedrin 93b asks why the book is not called by Nehemiah's name and answers that he took credit for himself, saying "My God, remember me for good" (5:19), and that he spoke badly of the governors before him (5:15). A defense: Nehemiah asks God, not people, to remember, and the prayer of 13:22 asks for pity according to God's loyal love, not according to his own merit. Christian readers have heard in it the thief's prayer, "Jesus, remember me" (Luke 23:42). In the Leningrad Codex, which puts Chronicles first among the Writings and Ezra–Nehemiah last, this line is the last sentence of the Hebrew Bible. The Aleppo Codex has the same order, but its last pages, with the end of Nehemiah, were lost after 1947.
